0.0-826.0 seconds: During the "carlot-triangle-dissection" phase of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the grasper steadily retracts the gallbladder—typically laterally, superiorly, and/or inferiorly—to optimize exposure of the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle, while a second instrument such as a hook, bipolar, or irrigator is methodically introduced to dissect, separate, and sometimes coagulate peritoneal, connective, fibrofatty, and areolar tissues surrounding the cystic duct, cystic artery, and cystic plate, progressively clearing attachments, expanding tissue planes, and delineating the critical anatomical structures of the triangle until the cystic duct, cystic artery, and the gallbladder’s interface with the liver are clearly defined and visualized.
837.0-988.0 seconds: During the clipping-and-cutting phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the grasper retracts the gallbladder to optimize exposure of the hepatocystic triangle, enabling the clipper to sequentially apply multiple clips across first the cystic duct and then the cystic artery, after which scissors are used to divide the cystic duct distal to the clips, leaving the clipped and divided structures clearly demarcated before instrument withdrawal.
998.0-1512.0 seconds: During the gallbladder-dissection phase, the grasper retracts and maintains tension on the gallbladder to expose the subhepatic dissection plane, while the hook is systematically and progressively used to dissect and separate connective tissue along the interface between the gallbladder wall and the liver bed—often advancing in both inferior-medial and superior directions, sometimes coagulating tissue as needed—which results in gradual mobilization and detachment of the gallbladder from its hepatic attachments and clarification of the anatomical boundaries until the gallbladder is fully freed from the liver surface.
